Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

source: original; stimulus table from Norris and Kristensen, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (2002), via Our World in Data

stimulus.source_note: Warhead counts: R. S. Norris and H. M. Kristensen, 'Global Nuclear Stockpiles, 1945-2002,' Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists (2002), via Our World in Data. Figures are approximate.
stimulus.text:
Nuclear warheads held, by year (approximate)

| Year | United States | Soviet Union |
| 1949 | 235 | 1 |
| 1955 | 2,422 | 200 |
| 1960 | 18,638 | 1,627 |
| 1965 | 31,139 | 6,144 |

stem: The growth shown in the table helps explain the policy of mutually assured destruction because

options.text: nuclear weapons had become useless and neither side feared them
options.misconception: Background from the books: both sides feared nuclear war deeply; the weapons were not seen as useless.

options.text: neither side could attack without facing devastating retaliation
the United States gave up its arsenal and trusted the Soviet Union
options.misconception: The table shows the American arsenal growing to 31,139 warheads by 1965, not being given up.

options.text: the Soviet Union agreed to disarm completely in 1960
options.misconception: The table shows the Soviet arsenal growing after 1960, to 6,144 warheads by 1965.

rationales.A: Background from the books: both sides feared nuclear war deeply; the weapons were not seen as useless.
rationales.B: Background from the books: with thousands of warheads on each side, any attack would bring a devastating reply, so the threat of reply deterred the attack itself.
rationales.C: The table shows the American arsenal growing to 31,139 warheads by 1965, not being given up.
rationales.D: The table shows the Soviet arsenal growing after 1960, to 6,144 warheads by 1965.
rationales.general:
1. The table shows both arsenals growing into the thousands of warheads.
2. A side that attacks would still face thousands of warheads in reply.
3. Background from the books: that certainty of reply is what mutually assured destruction means.
4. The policy therefore rests on the arsenals themselves, not on trust.
Remember: deterrence works when the reply is certain, not when the enemy is trusted.
